entries.value: GHK-Cu is not FDA-approved as a drug. Topical formulations are widely available as cosmetic products. Injectable forms are classified as research peptides. The compound's natural occurrence in human plasma provides inherent safety rationale but does not constitute regulatory approval.

GHK-Cu is not an FDA-approved drug. FDA's list of bulk drug substances nominated for compounding under section 503A (document updated 14 May 2026) places "GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration)" in Category 1, "Bulk Drug Substances Under Evaluation". FDA explains that GHK-Cu was removed from Category 1 on 22 April 2026 after the nominations were withdrawn. It was added back for non-injectable routes after one nominator clarified on 5 May 2026 that it meant to withdraw only the injectable route. Under FDA's interim policy, FDA generally does not intend to take action against 503A compounding with a Category 1 substance while the nomination is evaluated, if other conditions are met. This is enforcement discretion, not placement on the 503A bulks list and not an approval.

**Injectable routes:** FDA's page "Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding that May Present Significant Safety Risks" (content current as of 22 April 2026) lists "GHK-Cu (for injectable routes of administration)" under "Bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn". FDA's text reads: "Compounded injectable drugs containing GHK-Cu may pose risk for immunogenicity due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities. There are limited data in humans to inform safety-related considerations."

**Advisory committee:** FDA states that it intends to consult the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) "before the end of February 2027" on whether GHK-Cu could be included on the 503A bulks list. The PCAC meeting page (content current as of 15 April 2026) lists GHK-Cu on the agenda with LL-37, dihexa acetate, melanotan II and PEG-MGF, and says the meeting time and location will be scheduled. No date was posted as of 19 Oct 2026.
None of these listings is an approval. Advisory committee advice is non-binding, and Peptidemap does not predict the outcome.

entries.value: Multiple controlled clinical studies have evaluated topical GHK-Cu formulations for anti-aging applications. 12-week studies demonstrated significant improvements in skin firmness, elasticity, and density measurements compared to placebo.

Injectable (subcutaneous) GHK-Cu has not been tested on its own in any published human study found (PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov, 19 Oct 2026). The distinction between topical and systemic administration is significant: topical products deliver the compound to skin, and skin findings do not show what an injection does.\n\nNo human safety data for injected GHK-Cu given on its own were found. The only published human reports of injection involve multi-ingredient scalp formulations, so they cannot attribute any effect or adverse event to GHK-Cu. FDA states that "There are limited data in humans to inform safety-related considerations" for compounded injectable GHK-Cu.

Topical and injected evidence are different and must be kept separate. The published human studies of GHK-Cu itself are of topical cosmetic or wound-care products. No published human study of injected GHK-Cu given on its own was found in PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (searched 19 Oct 2026). Results from creams or serums do not show what an injection does, and results for injections cannot be inferred from skin studies.

**Pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia):** no completed, published randomised controlled trial of GHK-Cu itself was found, and ClinicalTrials.gov lists no GHK-Cu alopecia trial. The closest randomised trial tested a different substance, ALAVAX, a copper-free conjugate of 5-aminolevulinic acid and GHK. It was sprayed on the scalp in a double-blind, placebo-controlled 6-month study in men with male pattern hair loss (45 patients in the abstract). Mean hair count rose by 52.6 and 71.5 in the two active groups versus 9.6 with placebo; the only between-group difference reported as statistically significant was for the lower-concentration group versus placebo (Ann Dermatol 2016).

**Combination hair products:** other human hair reports tested multi-ingredient treatments in which copper peptide was only one component. These were an open-label, single-arm study of intradermal injections of a growth-factor formulation that included copper tripeptide-1 (J Cosmet Laser Ther 2018), and an uncontrolled clinic case series of 18,918 men given combination treatment that included an injected multi-ingredient solution containing copper tripeptide, alongside finasteride and minoxidil (J Clin Aesthet Dermatol 2018). Also in this group are a retrospective report of 7 men treated with minoxidil, dutasteride and copper peptides delivered by scalp micro-infusion (JAAD Int 2025) and four case reports of laser-assisted delivery combined with finasteride, growth factors and copper peptide (J Cosmet Laser Ther 2018). None of these isolates the effect of GHK-Cu, and none had a placebo group.

**Laboratory and animal hair studies:** a copper-binding peptide (PC1031) enlarged hair follicles in fuzzy rats (J Invest Dermatol 1993). A different copper tripeptide, AHK-Cu (not GHK-Cu), promoted the growth of human hair follicles in culture (Arch Pharm Res 2007). These findings do not show an effect in people.

**Skin:** in a study in which 13 patients completed after CO2 laser resurfacing, a topical GHK-Cu skin-care regimen made no significant objective difference to redness, wrinkles or overall skin quality, although patient-rated satisfaction was higher (Arch Facial Plast Surg 2006). A 2026 review concluded that "the clinical evidence remains sparse" (Pharmaceutics 2026). A phase 2 trial of a topical GHK-Cu gel for acute wounds (NCT07437586) is recruiting and has no posted results.
For injectable GHK-Cu, FDA states: "There are limited data in humans to inform safety-related considerations." See "FDA compounding status (as of 19 Oct 2026)".

key_points: Experimental studies link GHK‑Cu to increased ECM components (collagen, glycosaminoglycans) in wound models and altered expression of remodeling enzymes (MMPs) and their inhibitors (TIMPs)

Copper is an essential micronutrient and cofactor for multiple enzymes involved in connective tissue formation and antioxidant defense; a peptide that binds copper tightly may influence how copper is transported, buffered, or delivered to cells
Several animal and cell studies report reduced inflammatory cytokines and altered redox or stress signaling pathways following GHK‑Cu exposure
Computational and in vitro work has suggested GHK (and by extension interest in GHK‑Cu) may reverse certain disease‑associated gene signatures, particularly in lung disease research contexts

Evidence limits (as of 19 Oct 2026): no completed, published RCT of GHK-Cu itself for pattern hair loss and no published human study of injected GHK-Cu alone were found. Topical and injected evidence are not interchangeable. FDA lists GHK-Cu in 503A Category 1 for non-injectable routes only, and plans a PCAC meeting before the end of February 2027.

faqs.question: Is copper supplementation necessary with GHK-Cu?
faqs.answer: GHK-Cu is a copper complex of the tripeptide GHK; the copper ion is part of the complex. It is not studied or sold as a copper supplement, and this page gives no dose information.

faqs.question: Is there good human evidence for topical GHK-Cu on skin?
faqs.answer: Limited. Published human studies are small and mostly test cosmetic formulations. In a study in which 13 patients completed after CO2 laser resurfacing, a topical GHK-Cu regimen showed no significant objective difference in redness, wrinkles or skin quality, although patient satisfaction was higher (Arch Facial Plast Surg 2006). A 2026 review described the clinical evidence as sparse.

faqs.question: Is there a clinical trial of GHK-Cu for hair loss?
faqs.answer: No completed, published randomised controlled trial of GHK-Cu itself for pattern hair loss was found as of 19 Oct 2026. The closest randomised trial tested a copper-free 5-aminolevulinic acid–GHK conjugate, and other human hair reports used multi-ingredient products.

faqs.question: Has injected GHK-Cu been studied in humans?
faqs.answer: No published human study of injected GHK-Cu given on its own was found as of 19 Oct 2026. FDA states that there are limited data in humans to inform safety-related considerations for compounded injectable GHK-Cu.

faqs.question: What is GHK-Cu's FDA compounding status?
faqs.answer: GHK-Cu is not FDA-approved. FDA's 503A list (updated 14 May 2026) places GHK-Cu in Category 1 for non-injectable routes only; injectable GHK-Cu is listed as nominated but withdrawn on FDA's safety-risk page. FDA intends to consult its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee before the end of February 2027. Under FDA's interim policy, FDA generally does not intend to take action against 503A compounding with a Category 1 substance while the nomination is evaluated, if other conditions are met. This is enforcement discretion, not placement on the 503A bulks list and not an approval.

ghk-cu.conclusion:
GHK-Cu is a copper complex of the tripeptide GHK, which occurs naturally in human plasma. Laboratory, animal and gene-expression studies report effects on extracellular-matrix remodelling, inflammation and antioxidant pathways. These findings have not been confirmed in controlled human trials of systemic use.

The human evidence that exists concerns topical cosmetic and wound-care products, and a 2026 review described it as sparse (Pharmaceutics 2026). No published human study of injected GHK-Cu on its own was found, and FDA states that there are limited data in humans to inform safety-related considerations for compounded injectable GHK-Cu (as of 19 Oct 2026). Topical and injected evidence should be kept separate.

For researchers, GHK-Cu remains a well-characterised research compound with open questions about copper delivery, skin-repair mechanisms and whether any systemic effect exists in people. Readers should check the primary sources linked below before relying on any figure.

regulatory_subsections.title: Filing literacy — Lilly’s stated Q1 2027 filing plan (≠ approval)

entries.value: On 23 July 2026, Eli Lilly announced positive topline results from TRIUMPH-2 and TRIUMPH-3 and stated it is completing the comprehensive CMC data package required for a Biologics License Application (BLA) and plans to subsequently submit retatrutide in Q1 2027 for U.S. approval. That sentence is a sponsor filing plan.

Filing is not FDA acceptance (filing decision) and acceptance is not approval. Until FDA receives and files an application and assigns a review clock, there is no agency action date to treat as an approval date.
Do not convert “Q1 2027” into “approved in 2027.” Secondary timeline calendars that project review windows are estimates, not facts, and are not pasted here as predictions.

Later dated statements: Lilly’s 29 September 2026 announcement said it plans to submit a BLA in Q1 2027. On 2 October 2026, FDA concluded on remand that an application for retatrutide would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Lilly’s 8 October 2026 Seventh Circuit memorandum says it plans to file “no later than the first quarter of 2027” and needs to know which application pathway (biological product or drug) to pursue. See the classification subsection below.

regulatory_subsections.title: Biologic vs drug classification — FDA decision on remand (2 Oct 2026); Seventh Circuit appeal pending

entries.value: In January 2024, Lilly asked FDA to regulate retatrutide as a biological product under a Biologics License Application (BLA). FDA responded on 18 March 2024 that retatrutide is a drug, not a biological product. Lilly sued in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana (No. 1:24-cv-01503), which sent issues about whether retatrutide is “analogous” to a protein back to FDA. On 2 October 2026, deciding those issues on remand, FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research concluded that “retatrutide is not an analogous product to a protein and is therefore not a biological product. Accordingly, an application for retatrutide would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.” A redacted copy of the decision was filed in the Seventh Circuit on 8 October 2026 (No. 26-1301, Dkt. 46-2).

Lilly’s appeal in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, Eli Lilly and Company v. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., No. 26-1301, is from the district court’s judgment. The court heard oral argument on 24 September 2026 and ordered supplemental memoranda on appellate jurisdiction, which both sides filed on 8 October 2026 (Dkt. 45–47). In a footnote, Lilly’s memorandum says FDA’s new decision is “beyond the scope of this appeal” (Dkt. 47, n.3). As of 22 October 2026, no ruling appeared on the docket.

Educational takeaway only: under FDA’s 2 October 2026 decision, an application for retatrutide would be a section 505 drug application. Neither that classification decision nor the pending appeal is an approval decision, and an argument or a pending appeal is not a ruling.

regulatory_subsections.title: Access before approval — trials vs expanded access vs grey-market

entries.value: Before any approval, legitimate pathways discussed in primary manufacturer/FDA-process materials are clinical trials and, in limited circumstances, expanded access (sometimes called compassionate use) coordinated with a treating physician and applicable FDA IND / IRB requirements.

Lilly Medical states that retatrutide is not currently FDA-approved; that Lilly is supporting single-patient expanded-access requests for individuals who meet eligibility criteria when they cannot join a trial and have exhausted available options; that availability depends on geography, supply, and case-by-case assessment; and that requests are physician-initiated. ClinicalTrials.gov lists pre-approval expanded access as NCT07629401.

High-level eligibility themes on Lilly Medical include refractory obesity (BMI ≥35 despite highest tolerated approved chronic weight-management therapy), at least two serious or life-threatening obesity-related complications under standard care, and inability to join an ongoing retatrutide (or comparable) trial. This page does not turn those criteria into an application guide or medical advice.
Grey-market / RUO vials sold online are not clinical-trial supply and are not expanded access. Catalog adjacency is not a manufacturer program.

regulatory_subsections.title: U.S. Senate letter on “research use only” sales (14 October 2026)

entries.value: On 14 October 2026, nine U.S. senators (Jim Banks, Martin Heinrich, Ted Budd, Adam B. Schiff, Tom Cotton, Andy Kim, David H. McCormick, Jon Husted and Todd Young) wrote to Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas about online vendors that sell unapproved drugs and active pharmaceutical ingredients labeled “for research use only.” The letter uses “knockoff retatrutide” as its example and says: “We are concerned that ‘for research use only’ has become a dangerous loophole that undermines the FDA’s authority.” Sen. Banks’s office released the letter on 15 October 2026.

The letter urges FDA “to work more closely with U.S. Customs & Border Protection and other law enforcement agencies to take these illicit drugs off the market and hold the companies selling them accountable,” and requests a briefing on FDA’s enforcement strategy. It cites America’s Poison Centers data showing “a 265% increase in poisonings related to illicit retatrutide in the first four months of 2026 compared to the last four months of 2025.” PeptideMap has not checked that figure against an America’s Poison Centers release.
The letter is a request from members of Congress to FDA. It is not a law, a regulation or an FDA action, and it does not change retatrutide’s status: retatrutide is not FDA-approved.

NSW Health reported (19 Oct 2026) 1,180 presentations to NSW emergency departments associated with peptide use between 1 July 2025 and 30 September 2026. The release does not break this figure down by peptide. The release names retatrutide among the peptides that products may claim to contain and states: "None of these peptides are currently approved in Australia for any purpose."

No entry naming retatrutide was found in the Poisons Standard (October 2026; F2026L01327; in force from 1 October 2026). This page does not state a schedule for it. Not being named does not mean a product is unscheduled or may lawfully be supplied, and the NSW release states that retatrutide is not approved in Australia for any purpose.

entries.value: The Phase 2 trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023, showed retatrutide achieved up to 24.2% body weight reduction at 48 weeks at the highest dose — exceeding all previous results from any single pharmacological agent.\n\nThe compound was generally well-tolerated, with nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting as the most common adverse events (consistent with GLP-1-class effects). Phase 3 TRIUMPH results have since been published; see the TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2 subsections. Publication is not FDA approval, and those figures are not a dose.

TRIUMPH-2 (NCT05929079) was a registrational Phase 3 trial: 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and BMI ≥27 kg/m² were randomized to once-weekly retatrutide trial arms (4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg) or placebo for 80 weeks (EASD 2026 presentation; simultaneous Lancet publication, 29 Sep 2026). Figures below describe what was reported in that study — not how anyone should use research materials sold as RUO.

Efficacy estimand (Lilly press release, 29 Sep 2026) — models remaining on assigned intervention without prohibited weight-management treatments:

• 4 mg: mean weight change −12.7% (−29.8 lbs); A1C −1.4
• 9 mg: mean weight change −19.1% (−45.4 lbs); A1C −1.6
• 12 mg: mean weight change −20.8% (−49.6 lbs); A1C −1.5
• Placebo: mean weight change −4.0% (−9.3 lbs); A1C −0.2

Baseline averages cited by Lilly: weight ~106.4 kg, BMI ~38.2 kg/m², A1C ~7.7%. At 12 mg, Lilly reported 52.0% of participants achieving ≥20% weight reduction and 34.9% achieving ≥25% (efficacy estimand); 59.5% no longer met BMI criteria for obesity. Among participants with baseline BMI ≥35, mean loss at 12 mg was reported as 23.4% (60.8 lbs). Up to 40.0% reached A1C <5.7% (not family-wise type I error controlled per Lilly footnote).

Treatment-regimen estimand (Lancet abstract Findings): mean percent weight change −11.9% (4 mg), −16.8% (9 mg), and −18.8% (12 mg) versus −5.1% placebo (estimated treatment differences vs placebo −6.9%, −11.8%, −13.8%; p<0.0001 for all). Prefer stating which estimand you quote; do not mix them in one sentence without labeling.

Safety (Lilly): most common AEs vs placebo included diarrhea (27.4% / 33.5% / 33.6% vs 13.2%), nausea (13.7% / 20.8% / 28.0% vs 8.0%), constipation (14.0% / 16.2% / 16.8% vs 9.4%), decreased appetite (5.8% / 12.3% / 17.1% vs 4.5%), vomiting (5.5% / 10.2% / 15.7% vs 4.2%). Dysesthesia 4.5% / 5.6% / 7.3% vs 0.7%. Discontinuations due to AEs: 3.8% / 11.6% / 7.7% vs 4.9% placebo. Highest-dose CV risk-factor changes reported by Lilly included average reductions of 39.5% triglycerides, 19.6% non-HDL cholesterol, 10.8 mmHg systolic BP, 6.7 in (16.9 cm) waist circumference, and 58.3% hsCRP — risk factors, not CV outcomes from this trial.

human_use_subsections.title: TRIUMPH-1 Phase 3 (NEJM, 29 Sep 2026) — different trial from TRIUMPH-2

entries.value: TRIUMPH-1 (NCT05929066) is not TRIUMPH-2. Jastreboff and colleagues, for the TRIUMPH-1 Investigators, reported it in The New England Journal of Medicine (29 Sep 2026; DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2604169; PMID 42814954): adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, randomized to once-weekly retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg or placebo for 80 weeks (2,339 participants). The abstract states that, for weight-related endpoints, intercurrent events were handled by a treatment-regimen estimand. Under that analysis, mean percent change in body weight was −17.6% (4 mg), −23.7% (9 mg), and −25.0% (12 mg) versus −3.9% with placebo. Those abstract figures are the treatment-regimen result. They are not a treatment recommendation and not a head-to-head comparison with semaglutide, tirzepatide, or eloralintide. The same paper’s abstract does not print −28.3%. Lilly Medical’s table of TRIUMPH-1 outcomes, which cites that NEJM article, lists a separate efficacy estimand: percent change in body weight at 80 weeks was −19.0% (4 mg), −25.9% (9 mg), and −28.3% (12 mg) versus −2.2% with placebo. −28.3% is not the abstract primary weight result. TRIUMPH-2 remains the separate type 2 diabetes plus obesity or overweight trial; its published figures are not restated here and are not a ranking against TRIUMPH-1. PeptideMap is a research-use (RUO) comparison publisher, not a clinic or pharmacy. This is not medical advice and not a dose.

human_use_subsections.title: Reported safety signals outside clinical trials (as of 16 October 2026)

entries.value: This section summarizes reports about products sold under the name retatrutide outside Lilly's clinical trials. It is separate from the TRIUMPH clinical-trial results and does not change them. None of the reports below establishes that retatrutide caused any event. In most cases, the identity, content, and purity of the product involved are unknown. Products sold online under this name are not Lilly trial supply.

FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) death reports, as reported by CBS News. On 13 October 2026, CBS News reported that FDA had received two reports of deaths after people took products claiming to be retatrutide. CBS said it reviewed redacted FAERS reports obtained under the Freedom of Information Act. According to CBS, the first report (July 2026) described a 41-year-old woman who had cardiac arrest; the report listed retatrutide as a "suspect product" obtained "from an unreliable source." The second report (September 2026) described a 49-year-old patient who had severe dehydration, malnutrition, and cardiac arrest after buying the product from an online peptide vendor. CBS reported that it could not independently verify the reports, that FDA declined to say whether it had verified them, and that neither death was connected to a clinical trial. CBS also reported Lilly's statement that the reports "make clear the two individuals were taking black-market retatrutide." PeptideMap has not seen these reports. The public openFDA FAERS data (last updated 30 July 2026) listed 44 reports in which retatrutide appears as a drug name and no report coded as a death. That dataset predates the September report and may not yet include the July report.

Poison center exposures, as reported by CBS News. CBS reported that America's Poison Centers logged 862 retatrutide exposures in the three months ending in September 2026, 460 in the three months before that, and 249 in the first three months of 2026. America's Poison Centers began tracking retatrutide in late 2025. CBS noted that rising counts are common for a newly monitored drug. An exposure call is not a confirmed adverse effect. PeptideMap has not checked these figures against a public America's Poison Centers or NPDS release.

Limits of FAERS. FAERS is a spontaneous reporting system. Reports are not verified by FDA, can be incomplete or duplicated, and do not show that a product caused an event. For grey-market or "research use" products, the substance actually taken is usually unknown. Report counts cannot be used to estimate how often an event happens.

Social-media pharmacovigilance study (JAMA Network Open, 14 October 2026). Sehgal NKR, Tronieri JS, Rader B, Ungar L, and Guntuku SC published "Self-Reported Adverse Effects Among Social Media Users Taking Nonapproved Retatrutide" in JAMA Network Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38929). The study was a cross-sectional analysis of 148,640 retatrutide-related Reddit posts and comments. These came from 38,936 users across 27 communities, posted between May 2021 and December 2025. Large language models classified self-reported use and mapped the symptoms users attributed to retatrutide to MedDRA Preferred Terms, and the authors manually validated 100 posts. The models identified 13,589 users reporting current use. Of these, 7,823 had at least one mapped term after prespecified weight-loss and appetite-suppression terms were excluded. Among those 7,823 users, the most frequent terms were increased appetite (17.1%), fatigue (15.2%), increased energy (12.4%), nausea (11.6%), food craving (7.3%), insomnia (6.1%), and heart rate increased (4.8%). The authors note that gastrointestinal symptoms were common but not dominant, which differs from phase 2 trial findings.

Limits the authors themselves state: the findings are hypothesis-generating. Product identity, purity, dose, route, duration, concomitant medications, and medical history cannot be verified. Reddit users may not represent all users, and adverse events may be preferentially reported. The analysis cannot assess incidence, causality, dose-response, or comparative safety. The reported events may also reflect reconstitution practices, and natural language processing and MedDRA mapping may miss or misclassify symptoms. The reports may reflect product variability, peptide stacking, user characteristics, or misattribution. The study's comparison with semaglutide and tirzepatide was descriptive only, with unmatched samples and no statistical tests.
These reports describe unregulated products and cannot be compared directly with the controlled TRIUMPH trial safety data.

retatrutide.overview:
Retatrutide (LY3437943) is an investigational triple hormone receptor agonist (GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors) studied as a once-weekly injectable in clinical trials. cagrilintide.overview:
Cagrilintide is an investigational long-acting amylin analogue from Novo Nordisk. It is not approved in the US or EU, alone or in CagriSema (as of 19 Oct 2026). It is a lipidated analogue of amylin, a peptide hormone co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells (J Med Chem 2021). Novo Nordisk is developing it on its own and as part of CagriSema, a fixed-dose combination with the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide.

In the 68-week phase 3 REDEFINE 1 trial, adults with overweight or obesity assigned to CagriSema lost a mean 20.4% of body weight, compared with 3.0% on placebo (NEJM 2025). In REDEFINE 4, an 84-week open-label comparison, CagriSema did not meet its primary endpoint of non-inferiority to tirzepatide on weight loss (Novo Nordisk, 23 Feb 2026). Status as of 19 Oct 2026: Novo Nordisk submitted an NDA for CagriSema on 18 Dec 2025 and expects an FDA decision by late 2026. Cagrilintide alone is in phase 3 (the RENEW programme).
cagrilintide.background:
Amylin is a 37-amino-acid peptide hormone co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells (Pharmacol Rev 2015). Pramlintide (Symlin), a first-generation amylin analog, was FDA-approved for diabetes but has a short half-life (J Med Chem 2021).

Cagrilintide was developed by Novo Nordisk as a stable, lipidated amylin analogue designed for a long duration of action (J Med Chem 2021). In a phase 1b trial its human half-life was 159–195 hours (Lancet 2021). The development rationale was to pair amylin-pathway satiety signalling with GLP-1-pathway effects, which led to the CagriSema combination.

cagrilintide.human_use_intro: Cagrilintide has been tested in humans on its own and, mostly, as part of CagriSema. The results below come from peer-reviewed trial reports and Novo Nordisk company announcements, and each is labelled with its source. Figures from different trials are not directly comparable. This page gives no dose or schedule information.

entries.value: **Cagrilintide alone (phase 2; Lancet 2021, PMID 34798060):** in a 26-week dose-finding trial in 706 adults with overweight or obesity, mean weight loss ranged from 6.0% to 10.8% across cagrilintide dose groups, compared with 3.0% on placebo (trial product estimand). Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent.

**REDEFINE 1 (phase 3; NEJM 2025, PMID 40544433; NCT05567796):** 3,417 adults with overweight or obesity and without diabetes were randomised. At 68 weeks the mean change in body weight was −20.4% with CagriSema and −3.0% with placebo (estimated difference −17.3 percentage points; 95% CI −18.1 to −16.6; treatment-policy estimand). Gastrointestinal adverse events affected 79.6% of the CagriSema group and 39.9% of the placebo group and were mainly transient and mild to moderate.

**REDEFINE 2 (phase 3; NEJM 2025, PMID 40544432; NCT05394519):** in 1,206 adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, the mean change in body weight at 68 weeks was −13.7% with CagriSema and −3.4% with placebo (estimated difference −10.4 percentage points; 95% CI −11.2 to −9.5).

**REDEFINE 4 vs tirzepatide (phase 3, open-label; Novo Nordisk company announcement No 13/2026, 23 Feb 2026; NCT06131437):** in 809 adults with obesity, Novo Nordisk reported that "The trial did not achieve its primary endpoint of demonstrating non-inferiority on weight loss for CagriSema compared to tirzepatide after 84 weeks." Mean weight loss was 23.0% with CagriSema and 25.5% with tirzepatide if all people adhered to treatment, and 20.2% and 23.6% with the treatment-regimen estimand. These results come from a company announcement, not a peer-reviewed paper.

**Cagrilintide monotherapy in phase 3 (RENEW):** Novo Nordisk started a dedicated phase 3 programme for cagrilintide alone in Q4 2025. RENEW 1 (NCT07220642; placebo-controlled; about 300 participants) is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov as active, not recruiting, with primary completion expected in May 2027. No RENEW results have been published.
No REDEFINE or RENEW trial result is an approval. Long-term outcomes, including the REDEFINE 3 cardiovascular outcomes trial, are not yet reported.

cagrilintide.conclusion:
Cagrilintide is a long-acting amylin analogue whose main clinical programme is the CagriSema combination with semaglutide. Peer-reviewed phase 3 trials (REDEFINE 1 and 2, NEJM 2025) reported weight loss well beyond placebo. In REDEFINE 4, CagriSema did not show non-inferiority to tirzepatide (company-reported, 23 Feb 2026). As of 19 Oct 2026, neither CagriSema nor cagrilintide is approved. Novo Nordisk submitted an NDA for CagriSema on 18 Dec 2025 and expects an FDA decision by late 2026. No EU application was found, and cagrilintide alone is in phase 3.

For researchers, cagrilintide offers insight into amylin biology, which has been understudied relative to GLP-1 despite amylin's role in post-meal satiety and glucose regulation. Readers should check the primary sources linked below before relying on any figure.

faqs.question: How does cagrilintide differ from GLP-1 agonists?
faqs.answer: Cagrilintide acts on amylin receptors, which are calcitonin receptor complexes with receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMPs), while GLP-1 agonists act on the GLP-1 receptor (Pharmacol Rev 2015). faqs.question: Is cagrilintide FDA-approved?

faqs.question: What did REDEFINE 1 show?

faqs.question: Did CagriSema match tirzepatide in REDEFINE 4?

regulatory_subsections.title: U.S. regulatory status — compounding review (as of 19 October 2026)

entries.value: BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug, and no FDA policy permitting its use in compounding has been published as of 19 October 2026. In 2026 two separate U.S. steps concerned BPC-157 and compounding: an advisory committee vote in July and an interim policy sent for White House review in October. Neither one approves BPC-157 or makes it lawful to compound.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) met on 23–24 July 2026. On 23 July it considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the list of bulk drug substances that may be used in compounding under section 503A of the FD&C Act (the "503A Bulks List"). FDA evaluated both forms for ulcerative colitis. FDA's published voting questions were: "Should BPC-157 (free base) be placed on the list?" and "Should BPC-157 acetate be placed on the list?" In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither BPC-157 (free base) nor BPC-157 acetate be included on the 503A Bulks List. FDA states that advisory committee recommendations are non-binding. Reuters reported on 15 October 2026 that the advisers had recommended FDA loosen restrictions on six of the seven peptides reviewed in July, including BPC-157. As of 19 October 2026, FDA has not posted official minutes or vote tallies on the meeting page, so this entry gives no vote counts. The 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23) has not been amended to include BPC-157.

Interim access policy under OIRA review (received 14 October 2026). OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) lists a pending Executive Order 12866 review with these details (reginfo.gov, checked 19 October 2026; status "Pending EO 12866 Regulatory Review"). Title: "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides". Agency/Subagency: HHS / FDA. RIN: 0910-ZD94. Stage: Notice. Received Date: 10/14/2026. Legal Deadline: None. Economically Significant: No. The listing does not name any peptides and does not include the policy text. As of 19 October 2026, no matching Federal Register document and no FDA press announcement were found. Reuters, citing an Associated Press report based on two unnamed people, reported that the policy would allow some popular peptides, including BPC-157, to be compounded. That is a press report and has not been confirmed in any published text. Reginfo.gov also lists one EO 12866 meeting on this review, scheduled for 21 October 2026 and requested by the American Academy of Peptide Medicine. EO 12866 meetings let outside parties present their views to OIRA while a review is pending; a scheduled meeting is not a decision and does not indicate the outcome.
Not an approval: neither the PCAC vote nor the OIRA submission is FDA approval of BPC-157 for any use.
No published text: the policy text has not been released, and no Federal Register notice has been located.
No effective or start date: none has been announced.
Scope unknown: the OIRA listing does not say which peptides would be covered.
Review is not a final policy: an OIRA review is a step before publication. The policy may be changed, withdrawn, or published in a different form.

Other status lines are unchanged: on FDA's "Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding that May Present Significant Safety Risks" page (content current as of 22 April 2026), BPC-157 is listed as nominated but withdrawn. BPC-157 remains on WADA's S0 (non-approved substances) list.

WADA has banned BPC-157 for athletes under the class of "S0: Non-approved substances." This means athletes can face sanctions if caught using it in sport. The ban signals that BPC-157 is considered experimental and not recognized as a legitimate medication.
One attractive feature of BPC-157 in research is its apparently favorable safety profile in animals. Toxicology studies have found no lethal dose even at extremely high amounts:
In rats, a single injection of 20 mg per kilogram (a massive dose for a peptide) caused no deaths or obvious toxic effects
In dogs, daily injections for a month at doses up to 1 mg/kg showed no significant adverse effects compared to control animals
Studies reported no changes in body weight, behavior, or organ health attributable to BPC-157

The most prominent theoretical concern is BPC-157's ability to promote growth factors and blood vessel formation. While beneficial for healing injuries, this raises a question: could BPC-157 unintentionally help existing cancer cells grow or spread? Cancerous tumors often exploit the same pathways (like FAK/paxillin and VEGF) to invade tissues and nourish themselves with blood supply.

This idea is currently theoretical – no study has shown BPC-157 causes cancer in animals or humans. In fact, one lab test showed BPC-157 inhibited growth of a particular cancer cell line in culture. Nonetheless, experts urge caution until more is known about long-term effects.

bpc-157.regulatory_important_note:
"Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence" when it comes to safety. Because BPC-157 has not been extensively studied in people, there could be side effects that haven't been observed in small samples. Minor side effects like headaches, dizziness, or injection site reactions might not show up in tiny studies but could in larger populations.

Regulatory status (as of 19 October 2026): BPC-157 is not approved by FDA. A July 2026 advisory committee vote is non-binding. The "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" (RIN 0910-ZD94) has been under OIRA review since 14 October 2026. Its text has not been published, it has no effective date, and the peptides it covers are not known. PeptideMap does not predict outcomes.
key_points: BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide (15 amino acids) originally discovered in human gastric juice, with remarkable stability in harsh environments like stomach acid.
Preclinical research demonstrates significant healing potential for tendons, ligaments, muscles, bones, and gastrointestinal tissues through multiple biological pathways.
The peptide operates through pleiotropic mechanisms, increasing pro-healing factors (VEGF, nitric oxide) while decreasing inflammatory markers (COX-2, IL-6, TNF-α).
Human clinical evidence remains limited, with only small pilot studies conducted; BPC-157 is currently designated for research use only and is not approved by regulatory agencies.
The World Anti-Doping Agency has banned BPC-157 as a non-approved substance, and the FDA does not recognize it as a legal dietary supplement or drug ingredient.

Regulatory status (as of 19 Oct 2026): FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted on BPC-157 on 23 July 2026; the vote is non-binding. HHS/FDA sent an "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" to OIRA on 14 Oct 2026. No text has been published, no effective date has been set, and coverage is unknown. This is not an approval.

faqs.question: Has BPC-157 been tested in humans?
faqs.answer: Only in a few very small studies. A 2026 systematic review (Poolton et al., Acta Orthopaedica Belgica; PMID 42885452) found three human studies with 30 participants in total: a retrospective chart review of knee pain (16 people), a retrospective pilot study in interstitial cystitis (12 people) and a two-person safety pilot. None had a control group. The reviewers judged all three to be of poor methodological quality and rated the overall certainty of evidence as very low. These studies cannot show whether BPC-157 is effective or safe in people.

faqs.question: What does the animal research on BPC-157 show?
faqs.answer: Most BPC-157 research is preclinical, mainly in rats. A 2025 systematic review (Vasireddi et al., HSS Journal; PMID 40756949) included 36 studies, 35 of them preclinical, and reported improved healing outcomes in animal models of muscle, tendon, ligament and bone injury. Many of these animal studies come from the University of Zagreb group led by Predrag Sikiric, which first described BPC-157 in 1993 (McGuire et al., 2025; PMID 40789979). They are developer-affiliated, and readers should weigh them with that in mind. Animal results do not show that the same effects occur in people.

faqs.question: Is BPC-157 approved by FDA or allowed in compounding?
faqs.answer: No. BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug, and as of 22 October 2026 it is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23). FDA's page on bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks lists BPC-157 in its "nominated but withdrawn" table (substances previously in Category 2), not on the current Category 2 list, and the page still describes FDA's safety concerns. On 23 July 2026 a narrow majority of FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, according to press reports, voted to recommend adding BPC-157 to the 503A Bulks List. The vote is non-binding, and FDA has not posted minutes. A separate HHS/FDA "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" (RIN 0910-ZD94) is under OIRA review at the Notice stage. Its text has not been published, and it is not an approval.

faqs.question: Is BPC-157 prohibited in sport?
faqs.answer: Yes. BPC-157 is named as an example in class S0 (Non-approved substances) of the World Anti-Doping Agency's 2026 Prohibited List. Substances in S0 are prohibited at all times, in and out of competition.

It does not give dosing, route, timing, cycling, stacking, storage or sourcing guidance, and nothing on this page is medical advice. Products sold as BPC-157 "research chemicals" are not FDA-regulated drugs, and their content and purity are not verified.

To date, only minimal human testing has been published. A 2025 pilot study (Lee and Burgess, Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine; PMID 40131143), carried out at a private clinic in Florida, gave BPC-157 by intravenous infusion on two consecutive days to two adults who had received intravenous BPC-157 before. The authors reported no side effects and no measurable changes in the tested heart, liver, kidney, thyroid and blood glucose markers.

With two participants, no control group and three days of follow-up, the study cannot establish safety. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document for its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee notes that the published human studies of BPC-157 were of short duration, had small sample sizes and gave limited information on safety.

human_use_subsections.title: Registered Phase 1 Trial Without Published Results

entries.value: A Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers, PCO-02 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02637284, sponsor PharmaCotherapia), was registered in December 2015 to assess the safety and pharmacokinetics of BPC-157 oral tablets against placebo, with a single-administration part and a two-week repeated-administration part and an estimated enrollment of 42. The registry record was last updated in December 2015, its status is listed as unknown, and no results are posted. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document states that FDA was unable to find an associated published study.

Published human data on BPC-157 are limited to a few small, short studies. Most had no control group; the two placebo-controlled studies FDA identified (rectal enemas in healthy volunteers and in people with ulcerative colitis) are available only as meeting abstracts. A 2026 systematic review (Poolton et al., Acta Orthopaedica Belgica; PMID 42885452) rated the overall certainty of evidence as very low. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document concluded that there is insufficient clinical safety information to characterize the safety profile of BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate. Until controlled human trials are published, any human use is experimental.

findings.title: Wound and Muscle Healing
findings.content: Animal studies demonstrate accelerated healing of skin incisions and muscle tears when BPC-157 is applied. In rats with partially torn or crushed muscles, treated animals showed quicker healing and more complete muscle fiber regeneration compared to untreated controls in various research summaries.

findings.title: Tendon and Ligament Repair
findings.content:
In a rat model of transected (cut) Achilles tendon, a study by the Zagreb group that first described BPC-157 (Staresinic et al. 2003, Journal of Orthopaedic Research; PMID 14554208; developer-affiliated) reported better functional, biomechanical and microscopic healing measures in treated rats than in controls. A separate laboratory study (Chang et al. 2011, Journal of Applied Physiology; PMID 21030672) used rat tendon explants and cultured tendon cells and reported more tendon-cell outgrowth, better cell survival under oxidative stress and more cell migration.

These are animal and cell findings. They have not been tested in controlled human trials.

findings.title: Bone Healing
findings.content: A study in rabbits with non-healing bone defects found that local BPC-157 treatment was as effective as bone graft surgery in mending the defect. The peptide-treated rabbits showed new bone formation bridging the gap, similar to rabbits that received bone tissue transplants, suggesting BPC-157 may trigger regenerative processes in bone tissue.

findings.title: Gastric Protection
findings.content: BPC-157 was initially studied as a "cytoprotective" agent in the stomach, meaning it can protect stomach cells from injury. In rat studies, BPC-157 demonstrated the ability to prevent and heal stomach ulcers, including ulcers caused by NSAID painkillers, which are known for eroding the stomach lining. The peptide also protected the GI tract from alcohol-induced damage.

findings.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease Models
findings.content: Beyond the stomach, BPC-157 showed benefits in inflammatory bowel disease models. Rats with ulcerative colitis (a severe gut inflammation) recovered faster and had reduced intestinal damage when given BPC-157. A preliminary clinical trial in people with ulcerative colitis reported positive results, though full details have not been published.

findings.title: Anti-Inflammatory Effects
findings.content: In rat models of induced inflammatory arthritis, animals treated with BPC-157 had reduced joint swelling, less inflammatory cell buildup, and better preserved joint function than untreated rats. The peptide appeared to protect joints from autoimmune damage.

findings.title: Neuroprotection
findings.content: BPC-157 has shown promise as a neuroprotective compound in animal studies. It helped preserve brain cells in rodent experiments of traumatic brain injury and stroke, and produced antidepressant-like effects in a rat model of chronic stress. Rats with symptoms of depression or anxiety exhibited improved behaviors after BPC-157 treatment, correlating with modulation of serotonin and dopamine systems.

findings.title: Organ Protection
findings.content: In laboratory rodents, BPC-157 reduced damage to the liver caused by toxic chemicals and improved survival in cases of acute liver failure. Similarly, it lessened heart muscle damage in animal models of certain cardiac injuries, suggesting potential cardio-protective effects.

bpc-157.background:
BPC-157 was originally discovered in human gastric juice during gastroenterology research. In simple terms, a peptide is a short chain of amino acids – the building blocks of proteins. This particular peptide has been nicknamed the "body protection compound" in research circles due to the broad protective effects observed on the body's tissues in laboratory studies.

BPC-157 has been described as unusually stable for a peptide. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document cites a laboratory report that BPC-157 resisted breakdown in gastric juice in vitro (Veljaca et al. 1995). Routes studied in animals include intraperitoneal injection, oral administration by gavage or in drinking water, intravenous injection and intramuscular injection. FDA found no human pharmacokinetic data after oral, subcutaneous, nasal or transdermal administration; in small human studies of rectal enemas, BPC-157 was reported as not detected in plasma. Animal findings by any route do not show how BPC-157 behaves in people.

It's important to clarify that BPC-157 is an experimental compound. It is not approved as a medication by regulatory agencies and is officially designated for research use only at present. Despite this regulatory status, interest in BPC-157 has grown substantially due to promising early research findings in preclinical models.
bpc-157.conclusion:
BPC-157 stands out as a compound at the frontier of medical research. From a research perspective, it demonstrates several noteworthy characteristics: it's small and stable, has been studied by several routes in animals, and has shown remarkable healing capabilities in preclinical models across the board – from mending torn tendons to healing ulcerated gastrointestinal tissues and protecting neural cells.

However, a key message is caution. As of now, BPC-157 is not an approved treatment for any condition and remains in the realm of experimental research. The peptide is currently available only as a research tool, and any human use is essentially an off-label experiment.
